passages.happening:
‘Then three years passed without war between Aram and Israel’ (verse 1). In the third year Jehoshaphat king of Judah visits the king of Israel, who asks his servants, “Do you not know that Ramoth-gilead is ours, but we have failed to take it from the hand of the king of Aram?” (verse 3). He asks Jehoshaphat to go with him, and Jehoshaphat agrees, but asks first for the word of the LORD (verses 4-5).

The king of Israel gathers about four hundred prophets and asks whether to go. They answer, go up, for the Lord will give it into the king's hand (verse 6). Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there not still a prophet of the LORD here of whom we can inquire?” (verse 7). There is one, says the king of Israel, ‘but I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad’ (verse 8). He is Micaiah son of Imlah, and the king sends for him.

The two kings sit on their thrones in royal robes at the threshing floor by the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets prophesy before them. One of them, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah, has made iron horns and declares that with these the king will gore the Arameans (verses 10-11). All the prophets say the same: go up and prosper (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is the last chapter of 1 Kings and the end of Ahab, the king who has filled the book since chapter 16. Elijah has pronounced judgment on him for Naboth's murder, and God has delayed the disaster because Ahab humbled himself. Now the word is carried out, and another prophet speaks it.

The setting is about 853 BC. Israel and Aram had fought again and again. The three years without war fit what is known from Assyrian records: in 853 BC Shalmaneser III fought a coalition of western kings at Qarqar, and his inscription lists Ahab the Israelite, with a large force of chariots, beside the king of Damascus. Many historians think Ahab's last campaign came soon after, when the shared Assyrian threat had eased and old quarrels resumed. Ramoth-gilead was a fortified town east of the Jordan in Gilead, on a key trade route, and it changed hands between Israel and Aram more than once.

Kings consulted prophets before going to war, and a court could keep many of them. Ahab's four hundred speak in the LORD's name, but they are royal employees whose living depends on pleasing the king. Jehoshaphat seems to sense that unanimous flattery is not the same thing as the word of the LORD. Zedekiah's iron horns are a sign-act, a prophecy acted out; the horn was a common picture of a bull's strength and of royal power.
passages.later: Jeremiah warned against prophets like these: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They are filling you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16).
passages.asks: Ahab gathered four hundred voices that told him what he wanted, and hated the one who might not. Ask whom you avoid because they tell you the truth. And ask whether you are asking God for guidance, or only for permission.

passages.happening:
The messenger who fetches Micaiah urges him to agree with the others (verse 13). Micaiah answers, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever the LORD tells me” (verse 14). Asked by the king, he first echoes the prophets, and the king, hearing the irony, demands the truth (verses 15-16). So Micaiah says, “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd” (verse 17).

Then he tells what he saw: ‘I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left’ (verse 19). The LORD asks who will entice Ahab to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead. A spirit comes forward and says he will be a lying spirit in the mouths of all the king's prophets, and the LORD sends him (verses 20-22). “So you see, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the LORD has pronounced disaster against you” (verse 23).

Zedekiah strikes Micaiah in the face (verse 24). The king orders Micaiah held in prison on bread and water until he comes back safely (verses 26-27). Micaiah answers, ‘If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Micaiah's vision draws on the old picture of the divine council: God enthroned as a king among his heavenly court, deciding and sending out messengers. The two earthly kings on their thrones at Samaria's gate are set against the throne in heaven that Micaiah sees.

His first answer repeats the prophets' words with plain irony, and only when pressed does he tell the truth. His test is the one the law gives: whether the word comes to pass. The chapter sets four hundred prophets against one and shows that the title alone guarantees nothing.

The word for entice, patah, means to persuade, sometimes to deceive someone who is open to being deceived. The lying spirit is a spirit of sheqer, falsehood, a word Jeremiah uses for prophets who speak falsely in the LORD's name. A message can use the right name and still be false.

The man who told the truth is struck in the face and jailed.
passages.later: Moses had prayed that the LORD's people would not be ‘like sheep without a shepherd’ (Numbers 27:17). The law's test for a prophet was this: ‘When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken’ (Deuteronomy 18:22). Paul writes of people who refused the truth, that ‘God will send them a powerful delusion so that they believe the lie’ (2 Thessalonians 2:11).
passages.hard:
Does God lie or deceive people, as the lying spirit in Micaiah's vision seems to say?

The difficulty is real: Micaiah says the LORD sent a spirit to deceive Ahab through his prophets. Several things help. This is a vision of the heavenly council, told in the picture language of a royal court, and many interpreters read it as a vivid way of saying that God handed Ahab over to the falsehood he preferred, a judicial hardening like the one Paul describes in 2 Thessalonians. And the deception was not hidden. God tells Ahab the whole thing through Micaiah before the battle, so Ahab walks into it with his eyes open; he is warned more plainly than almost any king in the book. The prophets were already telling Ahab what he wanted to hear, and the spirit works through that.

Some interpreters stress God's direct rule even over evil spirits, as with the spirit that troubled Saul. Others stress that God permits the deceit rather than performs it. On either reading the text treats God as ruling over deception, not as a liar himself, since Micaiah tells the truth about the lie.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Micaiah would say only what the LORD told him, and it cost him. Ask whether you would rather be agreed with or told the truth. And ask what it would cost you to speak plainly in a room where everyone else has agreed.

passages.t: A disguise, a random arrow, and Ahab's death
passages.happening:
The two kings go up to Ramoth-gilead. Ahab says he will go into battle in disguise, while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes (verses 29-30). The king of Aram has ordered his chariot commanders to fight no one but the king of Israel. They chase Jehoshaphat, thinking he is the king, until he cries out and they see he is not (verses 31-33).

‘However, a certain man drew his bow without taking special aim, and he struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor’ (verse 34). Ahab tells his driver to take him out of the battle. The fighting goes on all day, and the king is propped up in his chariot facing the Arameans, ‘and that evening he died’ (verse 35). At sunset the cry goes through the army to go home (verse 36). They bury Ahab in Samaria. His chariot is washed at the pool of Samaria, and the dogs lick up his blood, ‘according to the word that the LORD had spoken’ (verse 38). His son Ahaziah reigns in his place (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Killing or capturing a king usually ended a battle, as the Aramean orders assume, and Ahab's disguise was a known tactic. The battle is full of reversal. The king in robes survives, and the disguised king is struck by an arrow shot at random. The Hebrew says the archer drew his bow in his innocence: he had no idea whom he was shooting. The arrow that kills the king is aimed by no one but God.

Ahab's death fulfills the judgment spoken for Naboth's murder, delayed but not canceled. God's patience in chapter 21 was real mercy, and Ahab spent it by going his own way.

Dogs in Israel were scavengers, and to have one's blood licked by dogs was a sign of utter disgrace. The text records it in a line and ties it back to Elijah's word.

The ivory palace of verse 39 has an echo in archaeology. Excavations at Samaria in the 1930s found many carved ivory panels that once decorated furniture and walls, and Amos later condemned the houses of ivory of Samaria's rich.
passages.later: Amos warned the rich of Samaria a century later: ‘the houses of ivory will also perish’ (Amos 3:15).
passages.asks: Ahab disguised himself to escape a word that God had spoken plainly. Ask what warning you are trying to outmaneuver rather than obey. And ask what it means that God's word reached a king through an arrow no one aimed.

passages.t: Jehoshaphat of Judah, and Ahaziah of Israel
passages.happening:
‘In the fourth year of Ahab’s reign over Israel, Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah’ (verse 41). He is thirty-five and reigns twenty-five years in Jerusalem (verse 42). He walks in the ways of his father Asa and does what is right in the eyes of the LORD, though the high places are not removed (verse 43). He makes peace with the king of Israel (verse 44) and drives out the male shrine prostitutes who remained from Asa's days (verse 46).

He builds ships of Tarshish to sail to Ophir for gold, ‘but they never set sail, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber’ (verse 48). When Ahaziah son of Ahab asks to send his men with Jehoshaphat's, Jehoshaphat refuses (verse 49). He dies, and his son Jehoram reigns (verse 50).

Ahaziah son of Ahab becomes king of Israel in Samaria and reigns two years (verse 51). He does evil, walking in the ways of his father and mother and of Jeroboam, ‘Ahaziah served and worshiped Baal, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done’ (verse 53).
passages.hearers:
Jehoshaphat reigned about 872 or 871 BC with his father Asa at first, and alone from about 870 to 848 BC. The narrator approves of him, though he did not remove the high places. His peace with Israel was sealed by the marriage of his son Jehoram to Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, an alliance that will draw Judah deep into the affairs of Ahab's house in 2 Kings, and Athaliah will later seize Judah's throne and nearly destroy David's line.

The note about the ships at Ezion-geber recalls Solomon's fleet (9:26-28). Chronicles tells the same episode differently, with Jehoshaphat in partnership with Ahaziah and a prophet condemning the alliance; interpreters usually suggest that verse 49 describes a second proposal after the first fleet was wrecked.

The book ends in the middle of things, with Ahab's son on Israel's throne and serving Baal. The story runs straight on into 2 Kings.
passages.later: Chronicles tells of the ships: ‘Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat’ (2 Chronicles 20:37), and the ships were wrecked. Matthew names Jehoshaphat in the line of David: ‘Asa was the father of Jehoshaphat’ (Matthew 1:8).
passages.asks: Jehoshaphat did right and still bound his house to Ahab's by marriage. Ask what alliance you have made that may carry your family further than you meant. And ask what you are leaving to those who come after you: a ruin, or a lamp.
